latent_mechanisms.display_name: Viral entry, systemic spread, or neural-ganglion reactivation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Enterovirus, herpesviruses, mumps, and other viruses reach the meningeal/CSF compartment through mucosal viremia, local neural reactivation, or parotid/respiratory viral spread without requiring bacterial invasion or brain-parenchymal necrosis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Viral antigen or replication burden in CSF-adjacent meningeal spaces
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Detectable viral nucleic acid or antigenic stimulation in the CSF/subarachnoid compartment drives aseptic inflammation; burden may already be low by the time lumbar puncture is performed.
Viral sensing in the periphery and CNS triggers fever, chills, malaise, myalgia, and modest systemic inflammatory marker changes that are usually less bacterial-shock-like than pyogenic meningitis.

Mononuclear/lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative bacterial Gram stain/culture, normal glucose, and elevated protein is the central measurable CSF phenotype; early illness can be neutrophil-predominant or only mildly pleocytic.

Inflamed meninges and mildly raised CSF pressure drive severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness or neck pain, nausea, vomiting, and pain with neck flexion even when classic Kernig/Brudzinski signs are absent.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Blood-CSF barrier permeability and protein leak
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Meningeal inflammation increases CSF protein and sometimes opening pressure or leptomeningeal enhancement while typically preserving CSF glucose because bacterial glycolysis and neutrophilic purulence are absent.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Herpesvirus persistence or recurrent reactivation context
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: HSV-2 and VZV can produce recurrent or reactivation-associated meningitis, sometimes without genital lesions or classic zoster rash; antiviral exposure reshapes this mechanism more than enterovirus or mumps disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Complicated CNS extension beyond isolated meningitis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: A minority develop encephalitic signs, cranial neuropathy, hearing loss, seizures, raised intracranial pressure, or neurologic disability; this mechanism remains low in uncomplicated viral meningitis and high values should push toward encephalitis or another CNS leaf.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Systemic viremia or herpesvirus reactivation seeds viral antigen into CSF-adjacent spaces.
Viral nucleic acid and infected-cell signals activate innate antiviral cytokine responses.
CSF viral antigen recruits lymphocytes and monocytes into the subarachnoid compartment.
Inflamed meninges directly generate headache, photophobia, neck symptoms, nausea, and vomiting.
Meningeal inflammatory permeability raises CSF protein and can produce mild leptomeningeal enhancement.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: mainly when HSV-2 or VZV context is present
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Latent herpesvirus reactivation and recurrence are a specific viral-context mechanism within the broader viral meningitis manifold.
HSV-2 or VZV reactivation can maintain PCR-detectable viral DNA and antigenic stimulation.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: more likely in neonates, older adults, immunocompromised hosts, VZV, HSV, or delayed evaluation
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: High or persistent viral burden can extend beyond isolated meningitis into encephalitic or cranial-neuropathy complications.
Systemic antiviral cytokines produce fever history, though afebrile presentations occur.
Measured temperature rises modestly in many but not all adult viral meningitis cases.
CRP can be mildly elevated but is usually lower than severe bacterial meningitis or sepsis.
Peripheral WBC may be normal or mildly elevated.
Systemic viral syndrome can include myalgia and malaise.
Malaise and fatigue often accompany viral CNS infection.
Severe headache is the dominant symptom of viral meningitis.
Meningeal irritation commonly produces photophobia.
Neck stiffness or pain with flexion may occur but classic signs are insensitive.
Meningeal irritation and raised pressure physiology can drive nausea or vomiting.
CSF inflammation is the parent finding behind pleocytosis and differential changes.
Viral meningitis generally causes CSF pleocytosis, ranging from very mild to hundreds of cells per microliter.
The mature CSF pattern is lymphocyte or mononuclear predominant.
Early enteroviral and other viral meningitis can be neutrophil-predominant before shifting to lymphocytes.
Blood-CSF barrier leak produces mild to moderate CSF protein elevation.
Opening pressure can be mildly elevated in viral meningitis.
Some viral meningitis cases show leptomeningeal enhancement, though imaging may be normal.
CSF glucose is usually normal in viral meningitis, unlike typical bacterial, fungal, or tuberculous meningitis; VZV can rarely be low.
PCR positivity is a direct virologic readout when the sampled assay matches the causative virus.
Ongoing untreated HSV/VZV persistence is inversely related to active antiviral exposure.
Confusion, encephalopathy, or persistent altered consciousness suggests extension beyond uncomplicated meningitis.
Seizures are uncommon in isolated viral meningitis and imply complicated CNS involvement.
Focal deficits should raise concern for encephalitis, vasculopathy, stroke, abscess, or another leaf.
VZV and other herpesviruses can produce cranial neuropathy or hearing symptoms.
Isolated viral meningitis should not create substantial parenchymal edema or mass effect; high values favor encephalitis, hemorrhage, abscess, or another CNS leaf.
Intracranial hemorrhage is not part of uncomplicated viral meningitis and should remain a rare complication-level hazard.
Complicated extension is the event pathway from meningitis toward encephalitic disease.
Opening pressure and inflammatory permeability can rarely progress to clinically important raised ICP.
Neurologic disability risk rises when disease is not isolated to meninges.
Mortality is low in uncomplicated viral meningitis but rises with encephalitic extension, immunocompromise, neonatal age, or severe complications.
Isolated aseptic meningitis carries low but nonzero short-term hazard from diagnostic delay, dehydration, and rare complications.

axes.clinical_baseline_context: Afebrile adults are common enough that fever absence must not exclude viral meningitis.
Enteroviral exanthem, mumps, HSV genital lesions, or VZV rash may be present, but VZV/HSV meningitis can occur without rash.
Mumps meningitis context; not required for viral meningitis.
Sustained confusion should push away from isolated viral meningitis toward encephalitis or another CNS process.
Early viral meningitis can be neutrophil-predominant; persistent very high neutrophil fraction is more bacterial.
Usually normal; VZV and other viral cases can rarely have hypoglycorrhachia.
Usually absent or low; high RBC should push toward traumatic tap, HSV encephalitis, hemorrhage, or other pathology.
Depends on virus, assay, and timing; negative PCR does not always exclude viral meningitis.
Should remain near absent in isolated viral meningitis; high values favor HSV encephalitis or another encephalitis leaf.

axes.display_name: MRI cerebral edema or mass effect activity
axes.clinical_baseline_context: Substantial parenchymal edema, midline shift, or mass effect should push away from isolated viral meningitis toward encephalitis, hemorrhage, abscess, tumor, or other structural CNS disease.
PCR, outbreak, season, and diarrheal/respiratory exposure context; modulates antiviral nonbenefit.
HSV-2/VZV PCR, recurrent aseptic meningitis, genital HSV, zoster, or zoster sine herpete context.
External diagnostic uncertainty context, not a viral disease mechanism; gates empiric antibacterial coverage while cultures/PCR are pending.
Higher in severely immunocompromised hosts with prolonged prior antiviral exposure.
High hemorrhage hazard is not a stable feature of viral meningitis and should favor HSV encephalitis, vascular disease, trauma, thrombocytopenic bleeding, or other hemorrhagic CNS processes.

axes.display_name: Encephalitis extension hazard in viral meningitis
Neurologic disability hazard in viral meningitis

axes.clinical_baseline_context: Low in uncomplicated immunocompetent adult viral meningitis; higher in neonates, immunocompromised hosts, encephalitic extension, or severe VZV/HSV complications.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Greater CSF inflammation usually travels with higher protein leak.

axis_couplings.conditionality: stronger after the first 24-48 hours of illness
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: The CSF differential often shifts toward lymphocytes after an early neutrophil phase.
Early neutrophil predominance and later lymphocytic predominance are temporally opposed parts of the same CSF differential.
Higher CSF pressure can worsen headache intensity.
Headache and photophobia co-vary as a meningeal irritation cluster.
Headache and neck stiffness co-vary but either can be absent.
Altered mentation is a key event-chain signal that disease is no longer isolated meningitis.
Seizures in this context strongly imply encephalitic or cortical involvement.
Extension into brain parenchyma or cranial nerves raises residual neurologic disability risk.
Clinically important ICP is rare but can raise mortality hazard.
If hemorrhage occurs in a viral-CNS context it raises mortality, but high hemorrhage also argues against uncomplicated viral meningitis.
The dominant mortality pathway is complicated CNS extension rather than uncomplicated aseptic meningitis.
Acyclovir crystal nephropathy can become clinically recognized AKI.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces symptomatic burden and dehydration while diagnostic testing excludes bacterial meningitis and HSV/VZV complications.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Acyclovir reshapes HSV/VZV replication and persistence but does not treat enterovirus or mumps meningitis.
Enteroviral meningitis is managed supportively; acyclovir has no meaningful antiviral target.
Acyclovir resistance can occur with prolonged herpesvirus replication in immunocompromised hosts.
Renal adjustment is required to preserve exposure while limiting neurotoxicity and nephrotoxicity.
Poor hydration increases crystalluria and AKI risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Crystal nephropathy risk rises with dehydration, renal impairment, rapid infusion, and high-dose exposure.
Creatinine can rise with acyclovir nephrotoxicity.

treatments.context_specific_role: Active vector for suspected or confirmed HSV/VZV meningitis, especially immunocompromised or severe presentations.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Valacyclovir has a rational target in HSV/VZV meningitis but not enterovirus.
Vomiting, ileus, malabsorption, or unreliable oral intake reduce CNS-active exposure.
Renal adjustment and neurotoxicity monitoring remain necessary.

side_effects.interpretation: Renal toxicity is less common than IV acyclovir but clinically relevant at high doses or impaired kidney function.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral option for stable HSV/VZV meningitis, step-down after IV therapy, or recurrent HSV-2 suppression decisions.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Foscarnet bypasses thymidine kinase activation and can retain activity against acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV.
Foscarnet is nephrotoxic and requires renal/electrolyte monitoring.

side_effects.interpretation: Foscarnet renal toxicity can limit exposure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rare rescue vector when herpesvirus meningitis is severe and acyclovir cannot provide active coverage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antibacterial coverage protects against a dangerous mimic while diagnostic data are pending; it is not a viral mechanism treatment.
Once viral cause and negative bacterial evidence are established, ongoing antibacterial benefit for the viral manifold is minimal.

treatments.context_specific_role: A safety bridge for suspected meningitis before bacterial disease is excluded; not a semantic first-line label for viral meningitis itself.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antiseizure therapy treats the complication, not uncomplicated meningeal inflammation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls seizures when complicated CNS extension is present; seizure occurrence should also trigger reassessment for encephalitis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ICP intervention is reserved for clinical or radiographic raised-pressure physiology.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rare escalation for raised ICP, hydrocephalus, or severe complicated CNS disease.

present.trajectory_modulation: Enterovirus, parechovirus, HSV, and severe systemic viral disease are more clinically important; fever may be subtle and complications higher.
Older adults have higher risk of VZV reactivation and complications; mimics such as bacterial meningitis, stroke, and temporal arteritis remain important.
HSV/VZV, chronic enterovirus, CMV, and atypical CNS infections become more likely; fever and CSF pleocytosis can be blunted while complications rise.
Persistent or relapsing enteroviral meningitis is more plausible, and PCR negativity can be misleading depending on timing and compartment.
Recurrent self-limited meningitic episodes increase HSV-2/Mollaret probability while not proving active HSV without CSF PCR.
Raises HSV-2 meningitis probability and makes acyclovir/valacyclovir biologically active; meningitis can still occur without visible lesions.
Raises VZV meningitis probability; rash can be absent, atypical, small, painless, or misattributed.
Summer/autumn seasonality, outbreak, daycare/school/household diarrheal or respiratory illness context raises enterovirus probability.
Mumps meningitis probability rises with parotitis, outbreak exposure, and absent/failed vaccination.
Does not define viral meningitis but changes antiviral toxicity and dosing geometry.

supportive_care: Perform prompt lumbar puncture when clinically safe; obtain opening pressure, cell count with differential, protein, glucose with paired serum glucose, Gram stain, culture, and targeted or multiplex viral PCR when available.
Do not use absent fever, absent nuchal rigidity, or mild CSF pleocytosis to exclude viral meningitis when severe persistent headache and CSF inflammation are present.

Use empiric antibacterial and acyclovir coverage when bacterial meningitis or HSV/VZV CNS infection has not been excluded, then de-escalate based on CSF profile, cultures, PCR, and clinical trajectory.
Provide hydration, analgesia, antipyresis, antiemetics, and observation for pain control, oral intake, and neurologic stability.
Monitor for encephalitic red flags: altered mental status, seizure, focal deficit, cranial neuropathy, progressive vomiting, papilledema, or abnormal brain parenchymal imaging.
Use renal-dose adjustment and adequate hydration for acyclovir or valacyclovir; monitor creatinine during high-dose or IV therapy.

Consider admission or prolonged observation for neonates, immunocompromised hosts, older adults, severe headache requiring parenteral analgesia, unreliable follow-up, or uncertain bacterial/HSV/VZV exclusion.
For enteroviral meningitis with stable neurologic exam and bacterial/HSV concerns resolved, supportive care and discharge planning may be sufficient.
For recurrent HSV-2/Mollaret context, counsel about recurrence, benign natural history in uncomplicated disease, sexual health evaluation, and individualized suppressive antiviral decisions.
Avoid anchoring on migraine or musculoskeletal neck pain when headache is persistent, severe, new, and accompanied by CSF inflammation.
distillation_quality_notes: Disease name is pure first-layer Viral meningitis; enterovirus, HSV-2, VZV, mumps, immunocompromise, and encephalitic extension are represented as mechanisms, axes, treatment modifiers, risks, or future subtype context rather than disease-name qualifiers.

Bacterial culture/PCR and herpesvirus/enterovirus PCR axes are allowed as test-result axes, but real case JSON can mark confirmatory microbiology as non-ranking when testing presentation-only diagnosis.
